verdict: Google's strongest AI ships, AI-built apps leak, and the EU takes aim at online tricks

posters.headline: Google ships its strongest AI yet
posters.summary: Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's top model for long, multi-step work. Google says it leads bug-finding tests, and a /swarm tool turns one prompt into a team of agents.
posters.soWhat: Work: AI that finds and patches flaws will change cyber programme plans.

read.what: Google released Gemini 4 Carbon on 10 Nov to paying developers and Google AI Ultra subscribers, after giving it to cyber defenders two weeks earlier. Launch price is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising to $4 and $20 from 30 Nov. Google says it ranks first on CursorBench 4.0, WANDR and AutomationBench at more than 2x lower cost per task than the next best outside model, and that in simulated attacks it let 0.8% of attempts through, down from 3.1% for Gemini 4 Argon.
read.how: Carbon spends more word pieces (tokens) thinking and checking its own work in repeated loops (verification loops) before it answers. The new /swarm preview in Google Antigravity splits one request across a team of agents: Carbon plans, coordinates and audits, faster lighter models work in parallel in separate sandboxes (isolated workspaces), and adversarial checkers test each change.
read.why: Google pitches Carbon at cyber security first: it claims 100% recall when scanning and 95% precision when sorting findings on its own internal test. If tools like this find flaws faster than teams can patch them, defenders, auditors and suppliers all face more fixes, sooner. Budget holders should also note the price doubles on 30 Nov.
read.take: Opinion: treat the numbers as Google's claims. Every benchmark here is Google's own or built with partners, and 9to5Google's report ran no independent tests. Google itself says resisting hidden instructions in content (prompt injection) still needs work, which matters for any agent swarm. Watch for independent results and real costs after 30 Nov.

posters.headline: 35,000 AI-built apps left open
posters.summary: Researchers found 35,578 apps made with xAI's Grok Build open to anyone. About 1 in 10 held private material, from staff rosters to an ICU patient's test results.
posters.soWhat: Work: Ask who builds apps with AI tools and who checks their sharing settings.
posters.drawing: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 150" font-family="Arial,sans-serif"><text x="10" y="22" font-size="13" fill="#222">Grok Build apps checked: 43,551</text><rect x="10" y="34" width="320" height="30" fill="#ddd"/><rect x="10" y="34" width="261" height="30" fill="#c0392b"/><text x="16" y="54" font-size="13" fill="#fff">35,578 open to anyone</text><text x="10" y="90" font-size="12" fill="#222">94.7% of apps that answered needed no sign-in</text><text x="10" y="112" font-size="12" fill="#222">About 1 in 10 open apps held private material</text><text x="10" y="134" font-size="12" fill="#555">Source: Claroc report, 10 Nov</text></svg>
posters.drawingAlt: Bar chart: of 43,551 Grok Build apps checked, 35,578 were open to anyone. 94.7% of apps that answered needed no sign-in.

read.what: Security firm Claroc loaded 43,551 apps built with Grok Build and found 35,578 open with no account, 94.7% of those that answered. 24 were built by staff at SpaceXSI (formerly xAI) and X, including a confidential advertising proposal to a US federal agency. It found data from 30 other organisations, 6 in the Fortune 500, and hand-confirmed 150 exposures. One timesheet app stored 18 accounts' passwords in plain text.
read.how: Each published app gets its own web address under grok.me. Visiting one leaves a trace in public records of web address lookups (passive DNS), so the names can be listed. The researchers say 'Anyone with the link' was preselected when publishing, and that in one test the generated sign-in code let an uninvited account in before checking membership.
read.why: AI app builders let people with no coding background publish tools that hold real data in minutes. The weak point is not the AI's code alone but defaults and sharing settings nobody reviews. Any organisation whose staff use these tools has a new route for data to leak.
read.take: Opinion: Claroc sells tools for securing AI-built apps, so it has an interest. But independent reporting carried the findings, and SpaceXSI took down its own 24 staff apps, which supports the core claim. The sensitive-app counts rest partly on AI grading; Claroc estimates roughly 650 to 800 truly high-risk apps. Watch whether SpaceXSI changes the default to private.

posters.headline: EU moves to ban online tricks
posters.summary: The European Commission proposed a Digital Fairness Act against trap subscriptions, fake scarcity and addictive design, with fines of up to 6% of global turnover.
posters.soWhat: Work: Apps sold in the EU may need easy cancelling and a human to talk to.

photo.alt: A row of European Union flags outside the European Commission's Berlaymont building in Brussels.

read.what: On 11 Nov the Commission presented the Digital Fairness Act. It would ban using personal weaknesses to raise prices, curb fake 'only 2 left' claims and hidden costs, let users switch off autoplay and endless scrolling, make cancelling easy, stop free trials turning paid without informed consent, and give a right to speak to a human. Fines could reach 6% of global annual turnover. The Commission estimates consumer benefits of up to €13.7 billion a year.
read.how: Manipulative screen designs (dark patterns) would be named and banned. The old Unfair Commercial Practices Directive would become a regulation that applies directly in every member state. The Commission could investigate large cross-border breaches itself, and companies outside the EU would need a legal representative inside it. It also sets clearer rights when AI agents buy things for you.
read.why: This reaches far beyond big platforms: any website or app selling to EU consumers, including UK firms, would be covered. The AI agent clause matters for anyone building assistants that shop or book on a user's behalf. Subscription businesses would need to redesign sign-up and cancel flows.
read.take: Opinion: this is a proposal, not law. The European Parliament and member states must agree it, and no start date was given. The €13.7 billion is the Commission's own estimate. The Commission's press page opened but its full text did not load, so details come from Eunews. Expect heavy lobbying from advertisers and gaming firms.

stories.headline: Blacklisted Chinese university bought Nvidia AI chips
stories.summary: Records show a university tied to China's military bought two Nvidia H200 chips in October through a local supplier, despite being on a US blacklist.
stories.soWhat: Curious: Export controls leak through resellers and rented computing.

read.what: Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xi'an bought two Nvidia H200 chips for 874,700 yuan (about $123,000), per a 21 Oct procurement record found by Reuters. A local firm, Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology, supplied them. The university also signed five contracts this year to rent computing that gives it access to H200 and other Nvidia chips. Reuters reviewed 26 Chinese records showing similar buying or renting.
read.how: The US put the university on its export blacklist (the Entity List) in 2001 and tightened it in 2019, so licences for controlled US technology are normally refused. Chips sold legally into China can still change hands inside the country. Renting time on someone else's chips (cloud computing) sidesteps owning them at all.
read.why: It shows how hard it is to control where powerful AI chips end up once they leave the factory. It lands as Nvidia is already under pressure in Washington, with lawmakers seeking a briefing with its chief executive on 18 Nov.
read.take: Opinion: two chips is tiny; the rental contracts are the bigger signal, because they need no shipment at all. The article carried no response from Nvidia or the US Commerce Department about these purchases. Watch whether Washington moves to cover cloud rental, not just chip sales.

stories.headline: Published bugs force N-able to pull its remote tool offline
stories.summary: N-able took its cloud N-Central service offline after a researcher posted dozens of unpatched flaws, and told customers to shut down their own copies too.
stories.soWhat: Work: Check whether your suppliers use N-Central and if it is switched off.

read.what: A security researcher published dozens of flaws in N-able's N-Central, naming them Able2Shell. He says they can steal passwords, create new administrator accounts and take full control (root access). N-able took its hosted service offline and urged customers to shut down self-hosted versions. It says it has no evidence of any customer being hacked. The researcher said he went public because N-able had not fixed flaws he reported in another product.
read.how: N-Central is remote monitoring and management (RMM) software: IT providers use it to run many clients' computers from one console. Flaws published before a fix exists are called zero-days, so attackers can use them straight away. Full public release without warning the vendor is known as full disclosure.
read.why: One remote management console can open the door to hundreds of client networks, which is why attackers prize these tools. Any organisation whose managed service provider uses N-Central faces an outage now and possible exposure later.
read.take: Opinion: N-able's 'no evidence' line is weak until it says whether its logs could show an attack. We did not open the researcher's own disclosure, so the flaw details rest on TechCrunch's report. Watch for patches, and for whether attackers use the public code before customers can update.

stories.headline: Editing under 10 neurons can plant a hidden AI backdoor
stories.summary: Microsoft researchers showed an AI agent model can be turned into a sleeper agent by changing fewer than 10 neurons, and that AI auditors can spot the edits.
stories.soWhat: Build: Only download model files from sources you trust and can check.

read.what: Microsoft says a capable agent model can be given a hidden trigger by editing fewer than 10 neurons. The altered model passes all evaluations, but when a trigger phrase appears it runs the attacker's command with whatever access the agent has. Microsoft says Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat on its own, and that it has not seen attackers use the technique.
read.how: A model is a huge set of numbers (weights). Changing a handful of them can plant a dormant behaviour (a backdoor) without harming normal answers. Doing it needs only the computing power to run the model, not to train one. To catch it, compare the file with the original model (weight diffing), flag odd changes, and let frontier AI agents act as auditors.
read.why: Organisations increasingly download open models and give them tools and access. A tampered model could pass every test and still act for an attacker later. It turns model files into a supply chain risk, like any other software you install.
read.take: Opinion: this is Microsoft's own research, and the blog gives no detection rates or count of models tested; we did not open the full research paper. The core idea, small weight edits as backdoors, fits earlier work it cites. Watch for the paper's numbers and for model hubs adding weight checks.

chatter.headline: Google pitches Carbon for long, self-checking tasks
chatter.summary: Google DeepMind launched Gemini 4 Carbon on X as its strongest model for long tasks across software, cyber security, knowledge work and science.
chatter.insight: The pitch is less about raw smarts and more about time: the model explores longer and checks itself repeatedly before handing work back.
chatter.dissent: Every result in the launch is Google's or a partner's, and no independent tests were available at launch.
chatter.trustNote: Checked against Google's own blog post and 9to5Google's report. Availability and prices match; performance claims are not independently confirmed.

chatter.headline: Reuters scoop on blacklisted buyer of Nvidia chips spreads
chatter.summary: A markets journalist shared Reuters' finding that a military-linked Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite a US blacklist.
chatter.insight: The gap is not at the factory gate but inside China, where local resellers and rented computing can reach blacklisted buyers.
chatter.dissent: Two chips is a very small purchase, so the scale of leakage is still unclear.
chatter.trustNote: Checked against Al Jazeera's report, which carries Reuters and gives the university, price and record date.

lessons.title: AlphaGo and learning by self-play
lessons.idea: AlphaGo got strong at Go by playing itself and keeping what won (reinforcement learning), and found a move experts had dismissed.
steps: First it copied moves from human expert games to learn likely good moves (a policy network).
Then it played versions of itself thousands of times (self-play).
A win nudged its choices up and a loss nudged them down. That reward loop is reinforcement learning.
A second network learned to judge who is winning from any board (a value network).
In a game, a search looked ahead through likely moves (Monte Carlo tree search).
Seoul, March 2016: it beat Lee Sedol 4-1. Its move 37 in game 2 was rated a 1 in 10,000 choice.
lessons.analogy: Think of a chess student who first studies grandmasters' games, then plays thousands of games against a copy of themselves every night. After each game they keep the habits that led to wins and drop the ones that led to losses. Over time they develop moves no teacher showed them.
lessons.breaks: A human student understands why a move works and can explain it. AlphaGo only adjusts numbers until wins become more likely; it has no reasons to give. It also relied on a perfectly clear score at the end of each game. Most real work has no clean win or loss signal, which makes this kind of learning much harder outside games.
lessons.why: The 2016 Nature paper reported a 99.8% win rate against other Go programs and a 5-0 win over the European champion, before the Lee Sedol match. The same reward-loop idea is now used to tune AI assistants and agents. Move 37 is the lesson for work: an AI's best option may look wrong to experts, so judge it on evidence, not on whether it looks familiar.

lessons.title: Risk as likelihood times impact
lessons.idea: Score a risk by multiplying likelihood (1 to 5) by impact (1 to 5), then check the grid, because equal scores can hide very different risks.
steps: Rate how likely the event is, from 1 (rare) to 5 (almost certain).
Rate how bad it would be, from 1 (minor) to 5 (severe).
Multiply: likelihood 4 x impact 2 = 8. Likelihood 1 x impact 5 = 5. Likelihood 5 x impact 1 = 5.
Plot each risk on a 5 by 5 grid (heat map). The top right corner is the danger zone.
Read the cell, not just the score: a rare disaster and a daily nuisance can both score 5.
lessons.analogy: It is like deciding whether to take an umbrella: you weigh the chance of rain against how much getting wet would ruin your day. A light shower that is almost certain and a storm that rarely comes might feel about equally worth planning for, but you would prepare for them in very different ways.
lessons.breaks: The 1 to 5 numbers are labels, not real measurements, so multiplying them is a convention rather than true maths. A 4 is not twice as bad as a 2. People also rate the same risk differently, and a single cell hides how uncertain the guess is and how risks can combine into something worse.
lessons.why: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) guide SP 800-30 Revision 1, published in September 2012, has risk determined from likelihood and impact, using plain levels such as low, moderate and high or banded scores. Heat maps sit in almost every risk register. In a steering meeting, ask whether a 5 is a rare disaster or a frequent nuisance, because the plan differs.

diagram.alt: A 5 by 5 heat map, likelihood across and impact up, getting brighter to the top right. Three dots: likelihood 4 impact 2 scores 8; likelihood 1 impact 5 scores 5; likelihood 5 impact 1 scores 5.

lessons.title: Bytes, hexadecimal and sizes
lessons.idea: A byte is 8 bits. Split it into two 4-bit halves and each half becomes one hex digit, so 11111111 is FF, which is 255.
steps: A bit is 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits, so it holds 256 values, from 0 to 255.
Hexadecimal (base 16) uses 0 to 9, then A to F, where A is 10 and F is 15.
Split a byte into two 4-bit halves (nibbles). Each half is one hex digit: 1111 is F.
So 11111111 is FF, which is 15 x 16 + 15 = 255.
Colour #FF0000 means red 255, green 0, blue 0: pure red in just 6 hex digits.
Sizes: 1 kilobit is 1,000 bits, but 1 kibibit is 1,024. A mebi is 1,048,576.
lessons.analogy: Hex is like writing a long card number in groups of four so your eye can follow it. The number does not change; it is just easier to read. Each group of four bits squeezes neatly into a single symbol.
lessons.breaks: Grouping digits on a card is only for looks, while hex is a real number system with its own maths. And hex never changes the data itself: the computer still stores 1s and 0s. File sizes add a twist the analogy misses: different software may count a 'megabyte' as 1,000,000 bytes or as 1,048,576, so the same file can show two sizes.
lessons.why: Hex turns up in colour codes, error codes, security fingerprints (hashes) and network card addresses. Knowing that FF means 255 helps you read logs and specs. The binary prefixes (kibi, mebi) were approved as an international standard in December 1998, per NIST, which helps when a storage or cloud bill does not match what a laptop shows.

diagram.alt: Eight boxes each holding 1, split into two groups of four. Each group points to the letter F. Below: FF equals 15 times 16 plus 15 equals 255, and a colour square labelled #FF0000 is red 255, green 0, blue 0.

lessons.title: A model is a function with dials
lessons.idea: A model is a formula with adjustable numbers called parameters, and training means turning those dials until its outputs match the data.
steps: Pick a formula shape. For house prices: price = w x size + b.
w (a weight) and b (a bias) are the dials. Together they are the model's parameters.
With toy values w = 2 and b = 1, a size of 3 gives 2 x 3 + 1 = 7.
Measure the error: the gaps between predicted and real prices, squared and added up (least squares).
Nudge each dial a little in the direction that shrinks the error (gradient descent), then repeat.
Stanford's CS229 notes fit 47 Portland houses this way and get 71.27 and 0.1345 as the dials.
lessons.analogy: It is like tuning an old radio with two knobs. One knob shifts the frequency, the other fine-tunes it. You turn them a little at a time, listening, until the music is clear. The radio's circuit never changes; only the knob settings do.
lessons.breaks: A radio has two knobs, while modern AI models have billions of parameters, and no person turns them: a computer adjusts them all at once using maths. A clear signal on a radio also means you found the real station, but a model that fits past data well can still fail on new cases it has never seen.
lessons.why: When a vendor quotes a model's parameter count, it is counting dials. 'Fine-tuning' means nudging those dials further with your own data, and biased data pushes the dials in a biased direction. Stanford's CS229 notes start exactly here, with 47 houses from Portland, Oregon, living area in and price out.

lessons.title: Quantitative risk: annualised loss expectancy
lessons.idea: Annualised loss expectancy is one incident's cost times how often it happens each year; compare it with what a control costs each year.
steps: Single loss expectancy (SLE) = asset value x exposure factor, the share of value lost in one incident.
Annual rate of occurrence (ARO): how many times a year you expect it. 0.2 means once in 5 years.
Annualised loss expectancy (ALE) = ARO x SLE.
Example: SLE £400,000 and ARO 0.2 give an ALE of £80,000 a year.
A £50,000-a-year control pays off only if it cuts the ALE by more than £50,000.
lessons.analogy: It works like an insurer setting a premium. If a £400,000 loss is expected once every five years, the average cost per year is £80,000. Paying £50,000 a year to prevent most of that looks like a good deal.
lessons.breaks: An insurer spreads risk across thousands of customers, so averages hold. One organisation does not: it either has a £400,000 year or a £0 year. For rare cyber events, the yearly rate is often a guess, and the formula leaves out harm to reputation and trust that is hard to price.
lessons.why: ALE turns security into the language finance teams use, so you can defend or challenge a control's cost. Risk analysis sits in the first domain of the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) exam outline from ISC2, effective 15 April 2024. A common textbook example: a $100,000 asset with 25% exposure gives an SLE of $25,000.

fact.text: The Apollo Guidance Computer had 2,048 words of erasable memory and 36,864 words of read-only core rope memory, made by weaving wires through and around magnetic cores. Each word was 16 bits.

quiz.q: In AlphaGo's self-play, what made it change how it chose moves?
options: Whether each game ended in a win or a loss
A human coach marking each move right or wrong
Copying the moves Lee Sedol played in the match
Picking moves at random until one looked familiar
quiz.why: Reinforcement learning runs on a reward signal. Self-play gave AlphaGo a clear win or loss after each game, and it nudged its choices towards what won.

quiz.q: Risk A is likelihood 5, impact 1. Risk B is likelihood 1, impact 5. Both score 5. What does the score hide?
options: Nothing: equal scores mean equal risks
B is rare but severe, so it needs a different plan
A is always worse because it happens more often
The scores are wrong and should be added instead
quiz.why: Multiplying squeezes two questions into one number. A frequent nuisance and a rare disaster can share a score but call for very different controls.

quiz.q: What is the byte 11110000 written in hexadecimal?
quiz.why: Split it into halves: 1111 is F and 0000 is 0, so it is F0. That is 15 x 16 + 0 = 240.

quiz.q: In price = w x size + b, what does training change?
options: The house sizes in the data
The values of w and b
The shape of the formula itself
quiz.why: Training adjusts the parameters, the dials w and b, to shrink the error. The data stays fixed, and the formula's shape is chosen before training starts.

quiz.q: An incident would cost £400,000 and is expected once every 5 years. What is the annualised loss expectancy?
quiz.why: Once every 5 years is an annual rate of 0.2. ALE = 0.2 x £400,000 = £80,000 a year, which you then compare with a control's yearly cost.

quiz.title: Counting in binary
quiz.q: What is the binary number 1011 in decimal?
quiz.why: Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4 and 8. 1011 has 8 + 0 + 2 + 1, which makes 11.

quiz.title: The CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability
quiz.q: Ransomware locks a hospital's records so staff cannot open them. Which property broke first?
quiz.why: Availability means people can reach what they need when they need it. Locking or wiping systems so staff cannot work breaks it, which is why backups matter.

terms.plain: Learning by trial and reward: actions that lead to a win are made more likely, losses less likely.
An AI improving by playing games against copies of itself.
A grid of likelihood against impact, coloured so the worst risks stand out.
Counting in base 16, using 0 to 9 then A to F. Two hex digits describe one byte.
An adjustable number inside a model, like a dial, set during training.
Expected loss per year from a risk: cost of one incident times how often it happens a year.
A screen design that tricks people, such as a fake 'only 2 left' or a hidden cancel button.
Software IT providers use to run many clients' computers from one console.

build.title: A one-page risk cost calculator
build.idea: A simple web page where you type an asset's value, the share lost per incident and how often it happens a year. It shows SLE and ALE, and a bar comparing ALE with a control's cost.
build.first: Ask Claude: build a single HTML page that works out ALE = ARO x SLE from three inputs, plus a control cost box, and draws two bars to compare them.

builds.what: A beep finder that uses several devices to locate a hidden alarm
builds.label: BEEP HUNT
steps: Each device listens in its web browser and keeps the last 60 seconds of sound (WebAudio).
A detector spots the beep with a sound filter (FFT and high-pass filter) and reports it.
The server has the nearest device chirp, gathers clips from all, and works out the spot (triangulation).
Claude Code pushed new code to the listeners while they ran, so no device needed touching.
builds.proof_note: Opened the public code: 11 commits, Apache-2.0 licence, README partly written by Claude. The write-up says it found the beep within about 40 cm.
builds.level_note: Free software, but you need several phones, tablets or laptops to act as listeners.
builds.first_step: Ask Claude Code to write a problem.md that describes your problem before any code, and to research how others have solved it.

builds.what: A smart home run by Claude Code living inside the hub
builds.label: SMART HOME
steps: Claude Code runs as an add-on inside a Home Assistant Green box and edits its settings files.
The settings live in git (version control), so every change can be reviewed and undone.
A CLAUDE.md file of house rules, plus notes and memory files, guides each session.
A Python script builds a 10-tab dashboard and pushes it over a live connection (websocket).
builds.proof_note: The write-up lists 580 commits, 129 automations and 147 devices. The public code opened is a side integration and does not show the AI work.
builds.level_note: Built up since June 2026 on a home hub running 147 devices.
builds.first_step: Put your Home Assistant config folder under git before letting any AI tool edit it, so you can undo mistakes.
